title_original: Lewis Baltz Research Fund #13 : Rebekka Deubner

blocks.text: The Lewis Baltz Research Fund #13 is awarded to Rebekka Deubner for the project tempête après tempête .

“For twelve years I have been traveling to Fukushima Prefecture at regular intervals to document the consequences of the nuclear accident on the ecosystem and on bodies. I focused on the more or less visible traces of 3.11*, a form of reshaping of the territory, while also taking an interest in the “normal” forms of life that persisted there. Then I met young people there who had experienced the triple disaster at a pivotal moment in their formation, giving rise to a hybrid portrait of local youth. Today I would like to examine the notion of reconstruction in the towns adjoining the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant. Beyond their specific history, they embody possible versions of our futures in spaces that humans have made uninhabitable. I would like to bring these temporal and spatial strata into dialogue in order to sketch the image of a territory where natural and industrial disasters, and their management, act as revealers.” — Rebekka Deubner

Rebekka Deubner was born in 1989 in Munich, Germany. She lives and works in the Île-de-France region. After studying art history and photography, she has exhibited her work at LE BAL, the Rencontres de la Photographie d’Arles, the MEP, the Fondation A Stichting and the Triennale Art & Industrie – Chaleur humaine in Dunkirk. Her work is represented by Les Douches la Galerie, where she is showing strip in 2026, examining filial memory through clothing and the body. In 2022 she was among the favorites (coups de cœur) of the prix LE BAL/ADAGP de la Jeune Création with her project carried out in Fukushima Prefecture on the triple disaster of March 2011. In 2025 she received the Bourse de l’Institut pour la Photographie de Lille to support the development of la terre amoureuse (said of earth that sticks to boots), which addresses water and the tensions surrounding it in the Deux-Sèvres and is exhibited at the Rencontres d’Arles in 2026. Publishing holds a central place in how her work is shaped and circulated, whether self-published or produced in collaboration with publishers such as Rotlux Press, September Books, Art Paper Editions and Sasori Books.
* 3.11 refers to the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster, which occurred on March 11, 2011, in Japan, following an earthquake and a tsunami.

The Lewis Baltz Research Fund was created to pay tribute to the American artist Lewis Baltz. It offers an annual grant supporting the creation, production and dissemination of an artistic or academic project, whatever its medium: book, performance, installation, video, film production or experimental digital work. Its aim is to support projects distinguished by their intellectual rigor, connected to the artistic approach of Lewis Baltz, who was close to political and societal questions.

Each year the laureate is chosen by the Lewis Baltz Research Fund committee: Diane Dufour, Florian Ebner, Theresa Luisotti, Mark McCain, Walter Moser, Slavica Perkovic, Thomas Zander and Matthew S. Witkovsky.
Initiated by LE BAL, the Lewis Baltz Research Fund is generously supported by Artworkers Retirement Society.

Since its creation in 2015, the Lewis Baltz Research Fund laureates have been: Alessandro Laita and Chiaralice Rizzi (2015), the artist duo Reichrichter (2016), Joanna Piotrowska (2018), Johann Lurf (2019), Tarrah Krajnak (2021), Theo Simpson (2021), Gabriela Löffel (2022), Jo Ractliffe (2022), Marina Gadonneix (2023), Hélène Giannecchini (2023), The Otolith Group (2024) and Andy Sewell (2025).

Lewis Baltz was born in Newport Beach, California. In the late 1960s, he began using photography to describe an increasingly impersonal world dependent on the logic of mass production. His images of industrial zones and of the exacerbated urbanization of the United States became symbols of postwar art, blending documentary vision and a conceptual approach. When he settled in Europe in the late 1980s, Lewis Baltz confronted a world in which globalization means the dematerialization of exchanges, precarious work and normative architecture. He then expanded his practice to video, confronting images and texts in installations.

His work has been the subject of numerous group and solo exhibitions, notably at the George Eastman House in 1975, the Whitney Museum of American Art’s Biennial Exhibition in 1977, MoMA PS1 in New York in 1991, the Art Institute of Chicago in 2010, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC in 2011, the Kunstmuseum Bonn and the Kestnergesellschaft Hannover in Germany in 2012, the Albertina in Vienna in 2013, LE BAL in Paris in 2014, MAPFRE in Madrid in 2016 and MAC’s Grand-Hornu in Belgium in 2017.
